query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the stability of a slow-growing, coherent oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the identity of the X element. In particular, when X is Al, the alloy tends to form a dual-phase oxide layer (chromia mixed with alumina) that relaxes interfacial stresses and enhances adhesion, while X as Si or Mn leads to oxide scales with higher growth stresses that crack or spall.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys (where X = Si, Mn, or Al) produced as single- or multiphase metallic solid solutions with homogeneous microstructures.
generation.intervention: Expose alloy samples to prolonged high-temperature (≥900 °C) oxidative or corrosive conditions.
generation.conditions: Testing is performed at temperatures above 900 °C in oxygen-rich or corrosive atmospheres over extended time intervals to assess oxide scale formation and integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature and continuity of the formed oxide scale—specifically, the presence of a dual-phase (chromia-alumina) layer versus a single-phase chromia with high internal stresses—mediates the alloy’s resistance to cracking and spallation.
generation.mechanism: The alloying element X influences oxygen diffusion, oxidation kinetics, and the development of interfacial stresses. Al promotes the formation of a mixed chromia–alumina scale that can dissipate growth stresses, improving adhesion at high temperatures. In contrast, Si or Mn do not generate such a stress-relieving phase, resulting in more brittle, stress-prone oxides that crack or spall.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature exposure, CrFeCoNiAl alloys will form a coherent, slow-growing, and adherent protective oxide layer, while the CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn variants will exhibit oxide scales that crack or spall due to higher interfacial stresses.
generation.baseline: A comparison with a baseline CrFeCoNi alloy that lacks the additional effect of the X element (or where X is present in a minimal amount) to establish that the enhanced stability in the Al-containing alloy is due to the deliberate selection of X.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys in their single- or multiphase metallic solid solution state when exposed to temperatures at or above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments for sufficient durations to develop observable oxide layers.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of oxygen diffusion kinetics and stress relaxation mechanisms, as well as the potential role of other minor alloying effects, remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with X = Al, Si, and Mn in comparable microstructural states. Expose all samples to an oxidative atmosphere at 950 °C for a fixed duration (e.g., 100 hours). Characterize the surface oxide layers using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and adhesion tests to assess oxide scale continuity, phase composition (i.e., presence of dual-phase chromia–alumina vs. single-phase chromia), and occurrence of cracking/spallation.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate
Phase composition and distribution within the oxide via XRD and electron microscopy
Adhesion quality (quantitative spallation or stress analysis) of the protective oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not exhibit a significantly more coherent, stable, and adherent oxide scale (with evidence of a dual-phase structure and lower cracking/spallation rates) compared to the Si and Mn variants under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified. Conversely, if the Si or Mn alloys also show comparable oxide scale stability, the proposed mechanism would be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Various stability criteria developed for high-entropy alloys are applied to compositions produced by mechanical alloying. While they agree with the annealed samples, these criteria fail to describe the as-milled metastable systems, highlighting the ability of mechanical alloying to overcome the limitations imposed by these criteria. The criteria are based on atomic size (Ω ≥ 1.1 and δr ≤ 6.6%) and/or electronegativity misfit, as well as on mixing enthalpy (Λ>0.95 J mol−1K−1 and −5 kJ mol−1<∆Hmix<0), or purely thermodynamic (ϕYe>20; ϕKing>1; Teff<500 K). These criteria are applied to several compositions found in the literature and to two metastable fcc solid solutions produced by mechanical alloying with compositions Al0.75CoXFeNi with X = Cr and Mn. Single-phase microstructures are stable up to above 600 K, leading to more stable multiphase systems after annealing above this temperature. Mössbauer spectrometry shows that, whereas the alloy with Cr is paramagnetic in the as-milled and annealed state, the alloy with Mn changes from paramagnetic to ferromagnetic behavior (Curie temperature ~700 K) after annealing. cited_evidence.text: Overall, the two six element alloys appear to be more promising candidates for forming low temperature HEAs than the two five element alloys. For AlCrMnNbTiV and AlCrMoNbTiV 17,830 (3.8%) and 17,289 (3.7%) out of 473,382 compositions sampled were single phase HEAs at 800 K. For AlCrFeTiV and AlCrMnMoTi only 356 (0.041%) and 785 (0.091%) out of 862,750 compositions sampled were single phase HEAs at 800 K. In Figure 6 and Figure 7 on average 64% and 67% of the grid points of the two-dimensional projections for AlCrMnNbTiV and AlCrMoNbTiV have circles on them, while in Figure 4 and Figure 5 these percentages are only 6.8% and 9.4% for AlCrFeTiV and AlCrMnMoTi. The supplementary material contains the list of compositions calculated and for each composition, whether that composition is a HEA at 800 K or not and what the phases and phase fractions are at 800 K for the four alloy systems.
